title: When Being Exceptional Starts Holding You Back
author: By Title Only
source: The Best Leadership Newsletter Ever, January 19, 2026
summary: The author uses the King Midas myth to illustrate how high-performing individuals struggle as leaders because they cling to the identity that made them successful. Exceptional workers often become leaders who micromanage, rewrite others' work, and require approval for decisions, effectively disempowering their teams. Real leadership transformation requires letting go of this identity and shifting from measuring worth by personal output to measuring it by how well others grow. The essay argues that when leaders release their grip on control, decision-making accelerates, innovation increases, and paradoxically, results improve.
points: Exceptional execution skills don't translate to leadership: The identity that made someone successful as an individual contributor becomes a liability in leadership. High-performing leaders must learn to measure worth differently.
The King Midas problem: Needing to touch everything to make it gold creates dependency, disempowerment, and stunts team growth. What feels like control is actually a curse.
Leadership is about transformation, not execution: Great leaders shift from creating results personally to enabling others to create results. They become gold miners, not gold makers.

Micromanagement is a symptom of identity issues: Rewriting emails, requiring approval for decisions, and always providing answers stem from a core belief that others can't do it as well. This trains teams to stop trying.
Letting go paradoxically improves results: When leaders stop being the hero and empower teams, decisions accelerate, innovation increases, and overall organizational performance improves.
quotes: The very thing that made me successful was the very thing that held me back. And it might be the same with you.
You're smart. You're talented. Everything you touch turns to gold. And that's the problem.
It's because the very thing that made me successful was the very thing that held me back.
The great leader is the one who no longer needs to turn things into gold with their own hands, because they've learned how to turn other people into gold miners.

When the exceptional leaders stop trying to be the hero, they learn to nurture the hero in others. That's when the winning happens.” Archived from The Best Leadership Newsletter Ever on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
